quests.sentence: The negotiations proceeded smoothly despite early tension.
quests.grammarRule: Manner adverb modifying a verb
quests.roleExplanation: 'Smoothly' is an adverb, not an adjective, because it modifies the verb 'proceeded' — describing how the negotiations went — rather than directly describing the noun 'negotiations'. A learner might mistakenly call it an adjective simply because it feels descriptive, but function, not feeling, determines the part of speech.
quests.nativeTip: A common mistake is assuming any word that 'describes' something must be an adjective. Ask instead: does this word modify the noun 'negotiations' directly, or does it modify the verb 'proceeded'?
quests.visualAnchor: 🚀 smoothly → Adverb (Manner adverb modifying a verb)
quests.example: The negotiations proceeded smoothly despite early tension.

quests.sentence: The smooth negotiations pleased both delegations.
quests.grammarRule: Attributive adjective modifying a noun
quests.roleExplanation: 'Smooth' is an adjective here, modifying the noun 'negotiations' directly — contrast this with the adverb use in the previous sentence, where the same root word modified a verb instead.
quests.nativeTip: Now compare: this word sits directly before a noun. What does it describe?
quests.visualAnchor: 🎨 smooth → Adjective (Attributive adjective modifying a noun)
quests.example: The smooth negotiations pleased both delegations.

quests.sentence: The dancer moved gracefully across the stage.
quests.grammarRule: Manner adverb modifying a verb
quests.roleExplanation: 'Gracefully' is an adverb modifying the verb 'moved', describing the manner of the dancer's movement — not a direct description of the dancer as a person.
quests.nativeTip: Remember: a word that describes how an action is performed usually modifies the verb rather than describing the person directly.
quests.visualAnchor: 🚀 gracefully → Adverb (Manner adverb modifying a verb)
quests.example: The dancer moved gracefully across the stage.

quests.sentence: Maria believes every word of the apology.
quests.grammarRule: Stative verb expressing a mental state
quests.roleExplanation: 'Believes' is a verb here, even though believing isn't a physical action you can observe — verbs can express mental states as well as visible actions.
quests.nativeTip: A common mistake is thinking words must show a visible action. Does 'believes' show something Maria does, even if you can't see it happening?
quests.visualAnchor: ⚡ believes → Verb (Stative verb expressing a mental state)
quests.example: Maria believes every word of the apology.

quests.sentence: Her belief in second chances never wavered.
quests.grammarRule: Common noun functioning as the subject
quests.roleExplanation: 'Belief' is a noun here, naming the conviction Maria held — it functions as the subject of the sentence.
quests.nativeTip: Check the words directly around it for clues. What never wavered?
quests.visualAnchor: 📦 belief → Noun (Common noun functioning as the subject)
quests.example: Her belief in second chances never wavered.

quests.sentence: The plan seems reasonable at first glance.
quests.grammarRule: Linking verb connecting the subject to a description
quests.roleExplanation: 'Seems' is a linking verb here, connecting 'the plan' to the description 'reasonable' — like 'believes', it shows no physical action but is still a verb.
quests.nativeTip: Remember: words don't have to show action. Does 'seems' connect the subject to a description, the way 'is' does?
quests.visualAnchor: ⚡ seems → Verb (Linking verb connecting the subject to a description)
quests.example: The plan seems reasonable at first glance.

quests.sentence: The company will spearhead the new initiative.
quests.grammarRule: Verb following the modal 'will'
quests.roleExplanation: 'Spearhead' functions as a verb here, meaning to lead — even though the word usually names an object (the tip of a spear), context shows it describes an action here.
quests.nativeTip: A common mistake is assuming a word is always a noun because it usually names a thing. Here, does 'spearhead' name an object, or does it show what the company will do?
quests.visualAnchor: ⚡ spearhead → Verb (Verb following the modal 'will')
quests.example: The company will spearhead the new initiative.

quests.sentence: The spearhead of the ancient weapon was remarkably well-preserved.
quests.grammarRule: Common noun functioning as the subject
quests.roleExplanation: 'Spearhead' is a noun here, naming the physical object — the pointed tip of the weapon — contrast this with the verb use in the previous sentence.
quests.nativeTip: Now compare: what physical object is being described as well-preserved?
quests.visualAnchor: 📦 spearhead → Noun (Common noun functioning as the subject)
quests.example: The spearhead of the ancient weapon was remarkably well-preserved.

quests.sentence: The critics panned the film relentlessly.
quests.grammarRule: Action verb in past tense
quests.roleExplanation: 'Panned' functions as a verb here, meaning to criticize harshly — a meaning that has nothing to do with the noun 'pan' used for cooking.
quests.nativeTip: Again, don't assume this is a noun just because 'pan' can name a cooking object. What did the critics do to the film?
quests.visualAnchor: ⚡ panned → Verb (Action verb in past tense)
quests.example: The critics panned the film relentlessly.

quests.sentence: The committee voted in favor of the proposal.
quests.grammarRule: Compound preposition introducing support for an idea
quests.roleExplanation: 'In favor of' functions as a compound preposition here, introducing an abstract relationship — support for the proposal — rather than a physical location.
quests.nativeTip: A common mistake is thinking words only show physical location. Does this expression show a place, or does it show support for an idea?
quests.visualAnchor: 📍 in favor of → Preposition (Compound preposition introducing support for an idea)
quests.example: The committee voted in favor of the proposal.

quests.sentence: Regarding your question, the policy hasn't changed.
quests.grammarRule: Preposition introducing a topic
quests.roleExplanation: 'Regarding' functions as a preposition here, introducing the topic being addressed — 'your question' — with no physical location involved.
quests.nativeTip: This word introduces a topic rather than a place. What topic does it introduce here?
quests.visualAnchor: 📍 Regarding → Preposition (Preposition introducing a topic)
quests.example: Regarding your question, the policy hasn't changed.

quests.sentence: Regarding your question, the policy hasn't changed.
quests.grammarRule: Common noun functioning as the subject
quests.roleExplanation: 'Policy' is a noun here, naming the official rule that remains the same — it functions as the subject of the sentence.
quests.nativeTip: Let the sentence, not the spelling, decide. What hasn't changed?
quests.visualAnchor: 📦 policy → Noun (Common noun functioning as the subject)
quests.example: Regarding your question, the policy hasn't changed.

quests.sentence: The results were promising; however, further testing is required.
quests.grammarRule: Conjunctive adverb showing contrast
quests.roleExplanation: 'However' is a conjunctive adverb here, not a true conjunction — it shows a contrast between the two ideas but cannot join them all by itself the way 'but' can; that's why the sentence needs a semicolon.
quests.nativeTip: A common mistake is assuming any word that connects two related sentences must be a conjunction. This word actually needs a semicolon before it, and it can move around within its own clause — true conjunctions can't do that.
quests.visualAnchor: 🚀 however → Adverb (Conjunctive adverb showing contrast)
quests.example: The results were promising; however, further testing is required.

quests.sentence: The results were promising, but further testing is required.
quests.grammarRule: Coordinating conjunction joining two independent clauses
quests.roleExplanation: 'But' is a true coordinating conjunction here — unlike 'however', it can join two independent clauses on its own with only a comma.
quests.nativeTip: Now compare: this word joins the two clauses directly with just a comma. What kind of word can do that?
quests.visualAnchor: 🔗 but → Conjunction (Coordinating conjunction joining two independent clauses)
quests.example: The results were promising, but further testing is required.

quests.sentence: The bridge was closed; therefore, traffic was rerouted.
quests.grammarRule: Conjunctive adverb showing result
quests.roleExplanation: 'Therefore' is a conjunctive adverb here, showing the result of the bridge closing — it behaves like 'however', requiring a semicolon rather than functioning as a true conjunction.
quests.nativeTip: Like 'however' earlier in this file, this word shows a result but needs a semicolon before it rather than joining clauses on its own. What kind of word behaves this way?
quests.visualAnchor: 🚀 therefore → Adverb (Conjunctive adverb showing result)
quests.example: The bridge was closed; therefore, traffic was rerouted.

quests.sentence: The company's decision surprised everyone.
quests.grammarRule: Possessive noun functioning as a modifier
quests.roleExplanation: 'Company's' is a noun in its possessive form here — it still names a thing (the company) even though it modifies 'decision'. Possessive nouns don't become adjectives just because they sit before another noun.
quests.nativeTip: A common mistake is assuming any word directly before a word must be an adjective. This word is still a word, just in its possessive form. What does it name?
quests.visualAnchor: 📦 company's → Noun (Possessive noun functioning as a modifier)
quests.example: The company's decision surprised everyone.

quests.sentence: The corporate decision surprised everyone.
quests.grammarRule: Attributive adjective modifying a noun
quests.roleExplanation: 'Corporate' is a true adjective here, describing the type of decision — contrast this with 'company's' in the previous sentence, which remained a noun despite modifying another noun.
quests.nativeTip: Now compare: this word has no possessive ending and exists only to describe. What quality does it give the decision?
quests.visualAnchor: 🎨 corporate → Adjective (Attributive adjective modifying a noun)
quests.example: The corporate decision surprised everyone.

quests.sentence: The team's strategy needed a complete overhaul.
quests.grammarRule: Possessive noun functioning as a modifier
quests.roleExplanation: 'Team's' is a noun in its possessive form here, naming the group that owns the strategy — it remains a noun despite functioning like a modifier.
quests.nativeTip: Remember: a possessive form is still the same part of speech as its base word. What does 'team's' name, even though it modifies 'strategy'?
quests.visualAnchor: 📦 team's → Noun (Possessive noun functioning as a modifier)
quests.example: The team's strategy needed a complete overhaul.

quests.sentence: "Well, I suppose we should get started," the host said.
quests.grammarRule: Interjection expressing hesitation
quests.roleExplanation: 'Well' functions as an interjection here, expressing the host's hesitation before starting — it stands apart from the sentence grammar entirely.
quests.nativeTip: A common mistake is assuming this word is always an adverb. Here it stands alone at the start, expressing hesitation rather than modifying anything. What role does it play?
quests.visualAnchor: 💥 Well → Interjection (Interjection expressing hesitation)
quests.example: "Well, I suppose we should get started," the host said.

quests.sentence: She hasn't been feeling well since Tuesday.
quests.grammarRule: Predicate adjective meaning 'in good health'
quests.roleExplanation: 'Well' functions as an adjective here, meaning healthy — it describes the subject's condition after the linking verb 'feeling', not the manner of an action. This is a common trap: 'well' is usually taught only as the adverb form of 'good', but it is also a true adjective meaning 'in good health'.
quests.nativeTip: Here 'well' describes a state of health after a linking verb, not how an action is performed. What is 'well' describing?
quests.visualAnchor: 🎨 well → Adjective (Predicate adjective meaning 'in good health')
quests.example: She hasn't been feeling well since Tuesday.

quests.sentence: He explained the process well enough for everyone to follow.
quests.grammarRule: Manner adverb modifying a verb
quests.roleExplanation: 'Well' functions as an adverb here, modifying the verb 'explained' and describing the quality of his explanation — the genuine adverb use, contrasted with the adjective and interjection uses seen earlier in this file.
quests.nativeTip: Now compare: this word describes how the explaining was done, modifying a verb. What role does it play here?
quests.visualAnchor: 🚀 well → Adverb (Manner adverb modifying a verb)
quests.example: He explained the process well enough for everyone to follow.

quests.sentence: This laptop is better than my old one.
quests.grammarRule: Predicate adjective in the comparative form
quests.roleExplanation: 'Better' is an adjective here, comparing the quality of two laptops — it is the comparative form of 'good'.
quests.nativeTip: This comparative word follows a linking verb and compares the quality of two things directly. What is being compared?
quests.visualAnchor: 🎨 better → Adjective (Predicate adjective in the comparative form)
quests.example: This laptop is better than my old one.

quests.sentence: She sings better than she used to.
quests.grammarRule: Manner adverb in the comparative form
quests.roleExplanation: 'Better' functions as an adverb here, modifying the verb 'sings' and comparing how well she performs — it is the comparative form of 'well', not 'good', in this context.
quests.nativeTip: A common mistake is assuming 'better' is always an adjective. Here it modifies a verb instead of a noun. What does it describe?
quests.visualAnchor: 🚀 better → Adverb (Manner adverb in the comparative form)
quests.example: She sings better than she used to.

quests.sentence: The traffic got worse during the storm.
quests.grammarRule: Predicate adjective in the comparative form
quests.roleExplanation: 'Worse' is an adjective here, describing the deteriorating condition of the traffic after the linking verb 'got' — the comparative form of 'bad'.
quests.nativeTip: This comparative word describes a condition after a linking verb. What condition did the traffic reach?
quests.visualAnchor: 🎨 worse → Adjective (Predicate adjective in the comparative form)
quests.example: The traffic got worse during the storm.

quests.sentence: Diego is a teacher at the local high school.
quests.grammarRule: Predicate noun functioning as a subject complement
quests.roleExplanation: 'Teacher' is a noun here, naming Diego's profession — it functions as a subject complement renaming 'Diego', not describing a quality the way an adjective would.
quests.nativeTip: A common mistake is assuming any word after 'is' must be an adjective. Does 'teacher' describe a quality, or does it name Diego's role?
quests.visualAnchor: 📦 teacher → Noun (Predicate noun functioning as a subject complement)
quests.example: Diego is a teacher at the local high school.

quests.sentence: Diego is patient with his students.
quests.grammarRule: Predicate adjective after a linking verb
quests.roleExplanation: 'Patient' is an adjective here, describing a quality of Diego's character — contrast this with 'teacher' in the previous sentence, which named his role as a noun.
quests.nativeTip: Now compare: does this word name a role, or does it describe a quality Diego has?
quests.visualAnchor: 🎨 patient → Adjective (Predicate adjective after a linking verb)
quests.example: Diego is patient with his students.

quests.sentence: The keynote speaker was a former astronaut.
quests.grammarRule: Predicate noun functioning as a subject complement
quests.roleExplanation: 'Astronaut' is a noun here, naming the speaker's former profession — it functions as a subject complement renaming 'the keynote speaker'.
quests.nativeTip: Again, don't assume every word after 'was' is an adjective. Does 'astronaut' describe a quality, or does it name a profession?
quests.visualAnchor: 📦 astronaut → Noun (Predicate noun functioning as a subject complement)
quests.example: The keynote speaker was a former astronaut.

quests.sentence: Well, the manager's decision, though surprising, proved better for morale than anyone expected, and productivity improved considerably.
quests.grammarRule: Interjection expressing a pause or reflection
quests.roleExplanation: 'Well' functions as an interjection here, signaling a reflective pause before the main statement — just like at the start of the sentence in an earlier lesson.
quests.nativeTip: Remember from earlier in this file: this word can stand alone at the start of a sentence, expressing a pause rather than modifying anything. What role does it play here?
quests.visualAnchor: 💥 Well → Interjection (Interjection expressing a pause or reflection)
quests.example: Well, the manager's decision, though surprising, proved better for morale than anyone expected, and productivity improved considerably.

quests.sentence: Well, the manager's decision, though surprising, proved better for morale than anyone expected, and productivity improved considerably.
quests.grammarRule: Possessive noun functioning as a modifier
quests.roleExplanation: 'Manager's' is a noun in its possessive form, naming the person who made the decision — it remains a noun despite modifying 'decision', just like 'company's' and 'team's' earlier in this file.
quests.nativeTip: Remember: a possessive form stays the same part of speech as its base word, even when it modifies another word. What does 'manager's' name here?
quests.visualAnchor: 📦 manager's → Noun (Possessive noun functioning as a modifier)
quests.example: Well, the manager's decision, though surprising, proved better for morale than anyone expected, and productivity improved considerably.

quests.sentence: Well, the manager's decision, though surprising, proved better for morale than anyone expected, and productivity improved considerably.
quests.grammarRule: Predicate adjective in the comparative form
quests.roleExplanation: 'Better' is an adjective here, comparing how the decision affected morale compared to expectations — following the linking verb 'proved', just like in an earlier lesson in this file.
quests.nativeTip: Remember from earlier: this comparative word can describe a quality after a linking verb. What is being compared here?
quests.visualAnchor: 🎨 better → Adjective (Predicate adjective in the comparative form)
